fetched_contents.text: History of Energy Labelling in the EU 1976 First EU measure regarding information on energy use of appliances The Council, following the Commission’s proposal, adopts a “Recommendation on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances”. For the first time, an EU measure addresses the issue of informing the public about the electricity consumption of appliances. The recommendation underlines the role of providing comprehensible information in encouraging purchase of the most energy efficient products. One of the recommended actions for the Member States is adopting measures regarding a standardized label, which would indicate the unit energy consumption of selected household appliances: water heaters, cookers, refrigerators, freezers and deep-freeze units, television sets, dishwashers, washing machines, dryers, spin dryers and ironing machines. * Council recommendation of 4 May 1976 on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances (76/496/EEC) 1979 First Framework Energy Labelling Directive and first EU-designed label The ground rules of the energy labelling framework are laid down. The first framework Directive provides for the general obligations of suppliers and dealers, while the details regarding each type of appliance are to be specified in implementing directives. However, unlike now, the energy labelling scheme is not mandatory/EU-wide: Member States may choose whether to oblige manufacturers and dealers on their territory to supply and display the labels. The appliances covered by the framework directive are: water heaters, ovens, refrigerators and freezers, washing machines, television sets, dishwashers, dryers, tumble dryers and ironing machines. The Directive includes a general template of the label. The first – and only – product group for which an implementing directive with a specific label is adopted is electric ovens: much smaller in size than the current labels, printed on an orange background and not showing an energy efficiency class of the appliance. Nevertheless, the key pieces of information first displayed on this label, energy consumption and usable volume of the appliance, are still included on the current oven energy labels. However, few Member States make the EU oven label mandatory. * Council Directive 79/530/EEC of 14 May 1979 on the indication by labelling of the energy consumption of household appliances * Council Directive 79/531/EEC of 14 May 1979 applying to electric ovens Directive 79/530/EEC on the indication by labelling of the energy consumption of household appliances 1990 Mandatory, EU-wide Energy Labelling Framework for selected household appliances The voluntary nature of the Energy Labelling framework is recognized as a potential obstacle to the implementation of internal market. Therefore, a new framework Energy Labelling Directive is adopted, and Member States are required to implement energy labelling measures for household appliances listed in the Directive: refrigerators, freezers and their combinations, washing machines, driers and their combinations, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters and hot-water storage appliances, lighting sources and air-conditioning appliances. Additionally, the Directive obliges the suppliers to provide a product fiche, corresponding to the current product information sheet. * Council Directive 92/75/EEC of 22 September 1992 on the indication by labelling and standard product information of the consumption of energy and other resources by household appliances 1994 First EU label under new framework introduces energy efficiency scale (refrigerators/freezers) A new label under the mandatory Energy Labelling framework is introduced for household electric refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations. The new design of the label is similar to the current one, with an energy efficiency scale now introduced. The idea of an energy efficiency class designated by a letter (where A is the most efficient class and G the least efficient one) and a colour (dark green for most efficient class and red for least efficient one) becomes popular and well recognised – and it is still used. * Commission Directive 94/2/EC of 21 January 1994 implementing Council Directive 92/75/EEC with regard to energy labelling of household electric refrigerators, freezers and their combinations 2010 Energy Labelling Framework for all energy-related products In the next step of the evolution of Energy Labelling framework, the possible scope of its application is extended from household appliances to all energy-related products (goods having an impact on energy consumption during use). The Commission is empowered to adopt secondary legislation for any type of such product, via delegated regulations directly applicable in any Member State under certain conditions. * Directive 2010/30/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 May 2010 on the indication by labelling and standard product information of the consumption of energy and other resources by energy-related products (recast) 2017 Current Energy Labelling Framework – the label goes digital The Energy Labelling Directive becomes a Framework Regulation. The Regulation adapts the rules previously developed in the Directive to technical and market developments and requires that the Commission establishes and maintains a product database. The EPREL database is developed by the Commission. Suppliers are now obliged to register each product model in the database and make its technical documentation available for national authorities verifying the products compliance with the energy labelling rules. fetched_contents.text: European Union energy label Energy consumption labelling scheme EU Directive 92/75/EC (1992)[1] established an energy consumption labelling scheme. The directive was implemented by several other directives[2] thus most white goods, light bulb packaging and cars must have an EU Energy Label clearly displayed when offered for sale or rent. The energy efficiency of the appliance is rated in terms of a set of energy efficiency classes from A to G on the label, A being the most energy efficient, G the least efficient. The labels also give other useful information to the customer as they choose between various models. The information should also be given in catalogues and included by internet retailers on their websites. In an attempt to keep up with advances in energy efficiency, A+, A++, and A+++ grades were later introduced for various products; since 2010, a new type of label exists that makes use of pictograms rather than words, to allow manufacturers to use a single label for products sold in different countries. Directive 92/75/EC was replaced by Directive 2010/30/EU,[3] and was again replaced by Regulation 2017/1369/EU from 1 August 2017.[4][5] Updated labelling requirements entered into force in 2021, the exact date depended on the relevant delegated regulation[6] (e.g. dishwasher's labels changed on 1 March 2021).[7] It reintroduced a simpler classification, using only the letters from A to G. The rescaling led to better differentiation among products that, under the previous label classification, all appeared in the same top categories. It meant, for example, that a fridge that previously had an A+++ label could now be a C category, even though the fridge is just as energy efficient as before. The main principle was that the A category would be empty at first, and B and C categories scarcely populated, to pave way for new, more energy efficient products to be invented and developed.[8] Major appliances Labelling The energy labels are separated into at least four categories: * The appliance's details: according to each appliance, specific details, of the model and its materials. * Energy class: a colour code associated with a letter (from A to G) that gives an idea of the appliance's electrical consumption relative to what is available on the market * Consumption, efficiency, capacity, etc.: this section gives information according to appliance type. * Noise: the noise emitted by the appliance is described in decibels. Refrigerating appliances For refrigerating appliances, such as refrigerators, freezers, wine-storage appliances, and combined appliances, the labelling is specified in terms of an energy efficiency index EEI, which is an indication of the annual power consumption relative to a reference consumption that is based on the storage volume and the type of appliance (refrigerator or freezer).[9] Refrigerating appliances, as EEI (post-2023) A B C D E F G ≤41 ≤51 ≤64 ≤80 ≤100 ≤125 >125 The label also contains: * the annual energy consumption in kW·h * the capacity of fresh foods in litres for refrigerators and combined appliances * the capacity of frozen foods in litres for freezers and combined appliances * the noise in dB(A) Pre-2021 For cold appliances (and this product alone), for models that are more economical than those of category A, categories A+, A++, and A+++ were previously assigned. According to the 2010 regulations, the boundary between the A+ and A classes was 44 up to 1 July 2014, and 42 after that date. ## Content and structure of energy efficiency labels

The EU energy label is designed to give consumers clear, comparable information on the energy efficiency of products. According to the evidence, the label includes an **energy class**, typically represented by a letter from A to G, with A being the most efficient and G the least efficient. This letter is associated with a **colour code**, which helps users quickly assess relative efficiency [N3-F3]. The label also provides **other useful information**, such as **annual energy consumption**, **efficiency ratings**, and, for certain products, **capacity**, **noise**, and other appliance-specific details [N3-F3].

The **format and presentation** of the label have evolved over time. The 1992 Directive introduced a general framework and a label template, but the format was not yet the modern EU label. In 1994, a new label was introduced for refrigerators and freezers, and it included an **energy efficiency scale** with a letter class and a colour code. This became the widely recognized design that still appears on current labels [N1-F1]. A major change in 2010 introduced a new label that uses **pictograms** rather than words, allowing manufacturers to use a single label across different countries [N3-R2]. The label was further updated in 2021, when **QR codes** became visible on labels, and a simpler classification was reintroduced using only the letters A to G [N3-F3]. The 2021 changes were intended to **reintroduce a simpler classification** and better differentiate products that had previously appeared in the same top categories [N3-F3].

The **product categories covered** include household appliances and energy-related products. The evidence lists **products covered by Directive 2009/125/EC and Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, including refrigeration, cleaning and drying, heating, cooling, ventilation, electronic products, light sources, tyres, and B2B products [N2-F2]. The 1992 Directive covered selected household appliances such as refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters, lighting sources, and air-conditioning appliances [N1-F1]. The 2010/30/EU framework expanded the scope to **all energy-related products**, defined as goods that have an impact on energy consumption during use [N1-F1]. The 2017 Regulation became the current Energy Labelling Framework and further extended the scope and required suppliers to register each product model in a **product database** [N6-R2].

There are **exceptions and special rules** for certain products. The evidence notes that the framework is not mandatory/EU-wide in its early stages; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. It also mentions that the label is required for **most white goods, light bulb packaging, and cars** when offered for sale or rent [N2-R3]. For refrigerating appliances, the label includes an **energy efficiency index (EEI)**, annual energy consumption, capacity details, and noise information [N3-F3]. Washing machines and tumble dryers have separate calculation methods and additional performance indicators such as washing performance and spin-drying efficiency, which were later simplified under the 2010/30/EU framework [N3-F3]. Light bulbs are also covered, with a notable transition in 2021 to a new system [N5-R5].

Overall, the label has moved from a simple energy consumption statement in 1992 toward a more complex and standardized format with pictograms, a broader scope, and digital elements such as QR codes [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The structure remains centered on **energy class, efficiency rating, annual consumption, and appliance-specific indicators**, while the **product categories covered** have broadened from selected household appliances to all energy-related products under the current framework [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R2].

## Chronology and major directive milestones

The history of EU energy efficiency labeling began with a 1976 Council recommendation on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances, which for the first time addressed informing the public about appliance electricity consumption [N1-F1]. In 1979, the first **Framework Energy Labelling Directive** was adopted, establishing the general rules of the framework, but it was **not mandatory/EU-wide**; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. The 1979 framework covered selected household appliances, including refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters, lighting sources, and air-conditioning appliances [N1-F1].

A major expansion came in 1992 with **Council Directive 92/75/EEC**, which made the framework **mandatory for selected household appliances** and required suppliers to provide a product fiche [N1-F1]. This directive laid the foundation for the modern label and product information system [N1-F1]. In 1994, the framework was extended to refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations with a new label design that introduced the **energy efficiency scale** using letters A to G and a colour code [N1-F1]. This became the popular and recognizable design still in use today [N1-F1].

The next major milestone was the **2010/30/EU Energy Labelling Framework**. This directive extended the scope from household appliances to **all energy-related products**, defined as goods having an impact on energy consumption during use [N1-F1]. It empowered the Commission to adopt secondary legislation via **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2010 framework also established a **harmonised system** for end-user information, particularly by means of labeling [N6-R1].

The current regime became a **Regulation** in 2017 with **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, which replaced the 2010/30/EU Directive and introduced a **digital framework**. The Regulation required the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database**, and suppliers were obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for verification [N6-R2]. The 2017 Regulation also introduced **QR codes** on labels, making the label more digitally visible [N3-F3].

Later updates followed. In 2021, the label underwent a major rescaling, reintroducing a simpler classification using only letters A to G and changing the way products were classified [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that the Commission is currently examining ways to simplify legislation on energy-efficient products, with a call for evidence on the Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU/2017/1369) and related rules [N5-F4]. This shows that the framework remains under active review, even as the 2017 Regulation has already become the current governing rule [N6-R2].

Each directive expanded or tightened requirements in a successive way: the 1976 recommendation introduced the idea of public information on appliance energy use; the 1979 framework established a general labeling structure; the 1992 Directive made it mandatory for selected appliances; the 1994 Directive added refrigerators and freezers with an energy efficiency scale; the 2010 framework expanded the scope to all energy-related products; and the 2017 Regulation digitized the system and added QR codes [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. The current framework is therefore a cumulative evolution, with each step broadening coverage, improving standardization, and adding digital and administrative layers [N1-F1][N6-R2].

## Legal and enforcement context

The legal basis for energy efficiency information requirements is rooted in the **Energy Labelling Framework**, which was established by **Directive 2010/30/EU** and later replaced by **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The current framework is described as setting out a **framework for energy-related products placed on the market or put into service** and providing for the **indication by labeling** and **standard product information** [N6-R4]. The 2010/30/EU Directive was itself a **harmonisation of national measures on end-user information**, particularly through labeling [N6-R1]. The framework therefore provides the **legal basis** for requiring suppliers and dealers to supply and display labels, and it is the main rule governing energy efficiency information across the EU [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Under the framework, the European Commission has a central role. It is empowered to adopt **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2017 Regulation also requires the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database** and to register each product model in that database [N6-R2]. Suppliers are obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. This shows that the Commission’s role is not merely advisory: it is responsible for **setting rules, maintaining a product database, and ensuring that product information is available for verification** [N6-R2].

Member States have **supervision and enforcement mechanisms** under the framework. The 1992 Directive required Member States to implement energy labeling measures for the listed household appliances, and the 2017 Regulation continues this obligation through the registration and verification system [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the Commission has organized **Implementation Dialogues** and **Reality Checks** to assess the current framework and prepare simplification proposals [N5-F4]. This suggests that enforcement and compliance are monitored through both national implementation and Commission-led review processes.

The European Commission and EU institutions interact through the **framework and delegated regulation mechanism**. The Commission adopts the **main framework regulation** and **secondary delegated regulations** that apply directly in Member States [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The Commission also interacts with market surveillance authorities, as suppliers must make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. The recent call for evidence on simplifying legislation indicates that the Commission is continuing to engage with stakeholders, including manufacturers, retailers, market surveillance authorities, and consumers, to assess the effectiveness and administrative burden of the framework [N5-F4]. This shows a collaborative enforcement model, with the Commission setting the rules, Member States implementing and supervising them, and national authorities verifying compliance [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-F4].

Overall, the legal basis is the 2010/30/EU Directive and the current Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, the Commission has the authority to adopt delegated regulations and maintain a product database, and Member States are responsible for supervision and enforcement, supported by national market surveillance authorities [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F4].

The EU’s regulatory system for energy efficiency labeling and information has evolved from a modest early recommendation into a broad, integrated framework covering household appliances and energy-related products. The development can be understood as a cumulative process of expanding scope, improving standardization, adding digital layers, and responding to market and climate policy needs. Across the branch reports, the evidence shows a consistent story: the framework began with a recommendation, then moved through early directives, the 2010/30/EU Energy Labelling Framework, and the current Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, with ongoing review and simplification efforts.

The earliest stage in the EU’s energy-efficiency labeling history was a **1976 Council recommendation** on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances. It laid the conceptual foundation for later directives.

A major milestone was the **1979 Framework Energy Labelling Directive**, which established the general rules of the energy labeling framework but was **not mandatory/EU-wide**; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. The directive covered selected household appliances and introduced a general label template, while specific implementation rules were left to later directives [N1-F1]. This marked the first formal EU-wide energy labeling framework.

The next key expansion came in **1992 with Directive 92/75/EEC**, which made the framework **mandatory for selected household appliances** and required suppliers to provide a product fiche [N1-F1]. This directive laid the foundation for the modern label and product information system [N1-F1]. In **1994**, the framework was extended to refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations with a new label design that introduced the **energy efficiency scale** using letters A to G and a colour code [N1-F1]. The directive empowered the Commission to adopt secondary legislation through **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. It also established a harmonised system for end-user information, particularly by means of labeling [N6-R1]. This was a major expansion because it moved the regime from a limited household-appliance set to a much broader product universe.

The current regime became a **Regulation** in **2017 with Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, which replaced the 2010/30/EU Directive and introduced a digital framework [N6-R2]. The Commission is also currently examining ways to simplify legislation on energy-efficient products, with a call for evidence on the Energy Labelling Framework Regulation and related rules [N5-F4]. Each step in this chronology expanded or tightened requirements in a successive way: the 1976 recommendation introduced public information on appliance energy use; the 1979 framework established a general labeling structure; the 1992 Directive made it mandatory for selected appliances; the 1994 Directive added refrigerators and freezers with an energy efficiency scale; the 2010 framework expanded the scope to all energy-related products; and the 2017 Regulation digitized the system and added QR codes [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. The current framework is therefore a cumulative evolution, with each stage broadening coverage, improving standardization, and adding administrative and digital layers [N1-F1][N6-R2].

---

## 2) Content and structure of energy efficiency labels

The EU energy label is designed to give consumers **clear, comparable information** on the energy efficiency of products. The evidence shows that the label typically includes an **energy class**, usually represented by a letter from **A to G**, with **A** being the most efficient and **G** the least efficient [N3-F3]. This letter is associated with a **colour code**, which helps users quickly assess relative efficiency [N3-F3]. The label also provides **other useful information**, such as **annual energy consumption**, **efficiency ratings**, and, for certain products, **capacity**, **noise**, and other appliance-specific details [N3-F3].

The **format and presentation** of the label have changed over time. In the early stages, the label was relatively simple, and the 1992 Directive established a general framework and a label template [N1-F1]. In 1994, a new label was introduced for refrigerators and freezers with an **energy efficiency scale**, introducing the now-familiar A-to-G letter class and colour code [N1-F1]. In 2010, a new label was introduced that used **pictograms** rather than words, allowing manufacturers to use a single label across different countries [N3-R2]. In 2021, the label was further updated with **QR codes** becoming operable on labels, and a simpler classification was reintroduced using only letters A to G [N3-F3].

The evidence also indicates that the **product categories covered** have broadened over time. The current framework covers products under **Directive 2009/125/EC and Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, including refrigeration, cleaning and drying, heating, cooling, ventilation, electronic products, light sources, tyres, and B2B products [N2-F2]. The 1992 Directive covered selected household appliances such as refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters, lighting sources, and air-conditioning appliances [N1-F1]. The 2010/30/EU framework expanded the scope to **all energy-related products** [N1-F1]. The 2017 Regulation further extended the scope and added digital requirements such as product registration and database use [N6-R2].

There are also **exceptions and special rules** for certain products. The evidence notes that the framework was not mandatory/EU-wide in its early stages; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. It also states that the label is required for **most white goods, light bulb packaging, and cars** when offered for sale or rent [N2-R3]. For refrigerating appliances, the label includes an **energy efficiency index (EEI)**, annual energy consumption, capacity details, and noise information [N3-F3]. Washing machines and tumble dryers have separate calculation methods and additional performance indicators such as washing performance and spin-drying efficiency, which were later simplified under the 2010/30/EU framework [N3-F3]. Light bulbs are also covered, with a notable transition in 2021 to a new system [N5-R5].

Overall, the label has evolved from a simple energy consumption statement in 1992 toward a more complex and standardized format with pictograms, a broader scope, and digital elements such as QR codes [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The structure remains centered on **energy class, efficiency rating, annual consumption, and appliance-specific indicators**, while the **product categories covered** have broadened from selected household appliances to all energy-related products under the current framework [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R2].

---

## 3) Legal and enforcement context

The **legal basis** for energy efficiency information requirements is rooted in the **Energy Labelling Framework**, established by **Directive 2010/30/EU** and later replaced by **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The current framework sets out a **framework for energy-related products placed on the market or put into service** and provides for the **indication by labeling** and **standard product information** [N6-R4]. The 2010/30/EU Directive was itself a **harmonisation of national measures on end-user information**, particularly through labeling [N6-R1]. This makes the framework the main rule governing energy efficiency information across the EU [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Under the framework, the **European Commission** has a central role. It is empowered to adopt **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2017 Regulation also requires the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database** and to register each product model in that database [N6-R2]. Suppliers are obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. This shows that the Commission’s role is not merely advisory: it is responsible for **setting rules, maintaining a product database, and ensuring that product information is available for verification** [N6-R2].

**Member States** have **supervision and enforcement mechanisms** under the framework. The 1992 Directive required Member States to implement energy labeling measures for the listed household appliances, and the 2017 Regulation continues this obligation through the registration and verification system [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the Commission has organized **Implementation Dialogues** and **Reality Checks** to assess the current framework and prepare simplification proposals [N5-F4]. This suggests that enforcement and compliance are monitored through both national implementation and Commission-led review processes.

The **Commission and EU institutions** interact through the **framework and delegated regulation mechanism**. The Commission adopts the **main framework regulation** and **secondary delegated regulations** that apply directly in Member States [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The Commission also interacts with market surveillance authorities, as suppliers must make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. The recent call for evidence on simplifying legislation indicates that the Commission is continuing to engage with stakeholders, including manufacturers, retailers, market surveillance authorities, and consumers, to assess the effectiveness and administrative burden of the framework [N5-F4]. This shows a collaborative enforcement model, with the Commission setting the rules, Member States implementing and supervising them, and national authorities verifying compliance [N1-F1][N6-R2][N5-F4].

Overall, the legal basis is the 2010/30/EU Directive and the current Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, the Commission has the authority to adopt delegated regulations and maintain a product database, and Member States are responsible for supervision and enforcement, supported by national market surveillance authorities [N6-R1][N6-R2][N5-F4].

## 4) Implementation and recent changes to labeling and product rules

Recent legislation and adopted updates affecting labels and product information are centered on the **Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** and the Commission’s ongoing efforts to simplify it. Under the 2017 Regulation, suppliers must register each product model in a **product database** and make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. The 2021 changes affected the classification system, which in turn affects how products are assessed and labeled [N3-F3]. The 2026 call for evidence suggests that the Commission is also looking at **minimum efficiency requirements** and how compliance can be made simpler, with a focus on preserving the effectiveness of existing rules while reducing administrative burdens [N5-F4].

**Transitional rules** are evident in the timeline of changes. The 2021 rescaling led to updated labeling requirements entering into force in 2021, with the exact date depending on the relevant delegated regulation [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that some changes, such as dishwasher labels, changed on **1 March 2021** [N3-F3]. This indicates that the framework uses **delegated regulations** to implement specific changes, which can create different effective dates for different product categories [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The Commission also organized an **Implementation Dialogue** and a **Reality Check** before launching the 2026 call for evidence, showing that transitional and implementation concerns are part of the legislative process [N5-F4].

The 2026 call also explicitly mentions the **Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** and the **Regulation on Tyre Labelling (EU/2020/740)**, showing that energy labeling is part of a broader product regulation ecosystem [N5-F4]. The Energy Efficiency Directive is also relevant, as it sets rules and obligations for achieving the EU’s energy efficiency targets and builds on previous EU energy policy [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The 2012 Energy Efficiency Directive was updated in 2018 and 2023, and it is described as the cornerstone of the EU’s energy efficiency policy [N4-R1][N4-R3]. This shows that energy labeling and product rules are not isolated; they are part of an integrated policy package that includes **ecodesign, energy efficiency targets, and market surveillance** [N5-F4][N4-R1][N4-R3].

In sum, recent changes have focused on **label rescaling, digital visibility, product database registration, and simplification of compliance rules**, with transitional dates and delegated regulations managing the rollout of changes [N3-F3][N5-F4]. The framework continues to interact closely with ecodesign and other product rules, and the Commission is using stakeholder input to refine the system [N5-F4].

---

## 5) Recent trends and future direction

Recent proposals or amendments affecting labels and product information are centered on the Commission’s call for evidence on simplifying legislation on energy-efficient products, launched in **February 2026**. This call is described as an **omnibus simplification** exercise that will assess existing rules, notably the **Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** and the **Regulation on Tyre Labelling (EU/2020/740)**, with a view to reducing administrative costs for businesses and improving compliance while preserving the effectiveness of existing legislation [N5-F4]. The Commission also explicitly mentions the recently agreed **Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU/2024/1781)**, indicating that simplification proposals are being prepared in the context of a broader sustainability framework [N5-F4]. This suggests a current trend toward **simplification, digital integration, and stakeholder consultation** rather than merely expanding the label itself.

The **impact of climate and sustainability goals** on labeling is clear. The Energy Efficiency Directive is described as setting rules and obligations for achieving the EU’s ambitious energy efficiency targets, and it is noted that the directive builds on previous EU energy policy [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The 2012 Energy Efficiency Directive was updated in 2018 and 2023, showing that the EU is continuously adapting its energy efficiency rules to meet climate objectives [N4-R1]. The Commission’s 2026 call for evidence also emphasizes that the label needs to be preserved while simplifying compliance rules, which reflects the tension between maintaining a strong regulatory signal and making the system more practical for businesses and consumers [N5-F4]. The evidence also notes that **83% of EU consumers** consulted the energy label when choosing products, indicating that the label is trusted and therefore valuable for sustainability messaging [N5-F4]. This makes it a key tool for aligning consumer behavior with climate goals.

**Uncertainties or open questions** about future changes include what specific simplifications will emerge from the Commission’s call for evidence, whether the label itself will change further, and how the new framework will interact with other product rules. The evidence does not provide the final wording of the proposed changes, only that the Commission is seeking stakeholder views on compliance, display, and the use of the **EPREL database** [N5-F4]. It also notes that the Commission is exploring whether to make better use of the **EPREL database**, which contains more than 2 million models of products with an energy label [N5-F4]. This leaves open questions about whether the label will become more data-driven, more digitally integrated, or more streamlined in its presentation [N5-F4]. Additionally, the Commission’s broader focus on sustainability suggests that future changes may be shaped by **ecodesign, carbon neutrality, and sustainable product policy**, rather than only by energy efficiency alone [N5-F4][N4-R1].

Overall, recent trends point to a future direction of **simplification, digital integration, and stronger alignment with climate and sustainability goals**, while the open questions concern the exact scope of the proposed changes and how they will preserve the label’s effectiveness and consumer trust [N5-F4][N4-R1].

---

## 6) Bottom line

The EU’s energy efficiency labeling and information regime has developed over time in a **cumulative and increasingly integrated way**. It began with a 1976 recommendation, moved through a series of directives and frameworks, reached its current form with the 2017 Regulation, and is now under active review for simplification and future adaptation. The system has expanded from a narrow household-appliance focus to cover **all energy-related products**, strengthened through **delegated regulations**, and digitized through **product databases and QR codes** [N1-F1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. It is also tightly connected to broader EU policy, including the **Energy Efficiency Directive** and the **Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation**, showing that labeling is part of a larger sustainability and market-regulation ecosystem [N4-R1][N5-F4]. In short, the EU has used energy labeling not only to inform consumers, but also to drive efficiency, standardization, and market coordination across the single market [N1-F1][N6-R1].

## Chronology and major directive milestones

The history of EU energy efficiency labeling began with a 1976 Council recommendation on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances, which for the first time addressed informing the public about appliance electricity consumption [N1-F1]. In 1979, the first **Framework Energy Labelling Directive** was adopted, establishing the general rules of the framework, but it was **not mandatory/EU-wide**; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. The 1979 framework covered selected household appliances, including refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters, lighting sources, and air-conditioning appliances [N1-F1].

A major expansion came in 1992 with **Council Directive 92/75/EEC**, which made the framework **mandatory for selected household appliances** and required suppliers to provide a product fiche [N1-F1]. This directive laid the foundation for the modern label and product information system [N1-F1]. In 1994, the framework was extended to refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations with a new label design that introduced the **energy efficiency scale** using letters A to G and a colour code [N1-F1]. This became the popular and recognizable design still in use today [N1-F1].

The next major milestone was the **2010/30/EU Energy Labelling Framework**. This directive extended the scope from household appliances to **all energy-related products**, defined as goods having an impact on energy consumption during use [N1-F1]. It empowered the Commission to adopt secondary legislation via **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2010 framework also established a **harmonised system** for end-user information, particularly by means of labeling [N6-R1].

The current regime became a **Regulation** in 2017 with **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, which replaced the 2010/30/EU Directive and introduced a **digital framework**. The Regulation required the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database**, and suppliers were obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for verification [N6-R2]. The 2017 Regulation also introduced **QR codes** on labels, making the label more digitally visible [N3-F3].

Later updates followed. In 2021, the label underwent a major rescaling, reintroducing a simpler classification using only letters A to G and changing the way products were classified [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that the Commission is currently examining ways to simplify legislation on energy-efficient products, with a call for evidence on the Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU/2017/1369) and related rules [N5-F4]. This shows that the framework remains under active review, even as the 2017 Regulation has already become the current governing rule [N6-R2].

Each directive expanded or tightened requirements in a successive way: the 1976 recommendation introduced the idea of public information on appliance energy use; the 1979 framework established a general labeling structure; the 1992 Directive made it mandatory for selected appliances; the 1994 Directive added refrigerators and freezers with an energy efficiency scale; the 2010 framework expanded the scope to all energy-related products; and the 2017 Regulation digitized the system and added QR codes [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. The current framework is therefore a cumulative evolution, with each step broadening coverage, improving standardization, and adding digital and administrative layers [N1-F1][N6-R2].

## Chronology and major directive milestones

The history of EU energy efficiency labeling began with a 1976 Council recommendation on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances, which for the first time addressed informing the public about appliance electricity consumption [N1-F1]. In 1979, the first **Framework Energy Labelling Directive** was adopted, establishing the general rules of the framework, but it was **not mandatory/EU-wide**; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. The 1979 framework covered selected household appliances, including refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, water heaters, lighting sources, and air-conditioning appliances [N1-F1].

A major expansion came in 1992 with **Council Directive 92/75/EEC**, which made the framework **mandatory for selected household appliances** and required suppliers to provide a product fiche [N1-F1]. This directive laid the foundation for the modern label and product information system [N1-F1]. In 1994, the framework was extended to refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations with a new label design that introduced the **energy efficiency scale** using letters A to G and a colour code [N1-F1]. This became the popular and recognizable design still in use today [N1-F1].

The next major milestone was the **2010/30/EU Energy Labelling Framework**. This directive extended the scope from household appliances to **all energy-related products**, defined as goods having an impact on energy consumption during use [N1-F1]. It empowered the Commission to adopt secondary legislation via **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2010 framework also established a **harmonised system** for end-user information, particularly by means of labeling [N6-R1].

The current regime became a **Regulation** in 2017 with **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, which replaced the 2010/30/EU Directive and introduced a **digital framework**. The Regulation required the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database**, and suppliers were obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for verification [N6-R2]. The 2017 Regulation also introduced **QR codes** on labels, making the label more digitally visible [N3-F3].

Later updates followed. In 2021, the label underwent a major rescaling, reintroducing a simpler classification using only letters A to G and changing the way products were classified [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that the Commission is currently examining ways to simplify legislation on energy-efficient products, with a call for evidence on the Energy Labelling Framework Regulation (EU/2017/1369) and related rules [N5-F4]. This shows that the framework remains under active review, even as the 2017 Regulation has already become the current governing rule [N6-R2].

Each directive expanded or tightened requirements in a successive way: the 1976 recommendation introduced the idea of public information on appliance energy use; the 1979 framework established a general labeling structure; the 1992 Directive made it mandatory for selected appliances; the 1994 Directive added refrigerators and freezers with an energy efficiency scale; the 2010 framework expanded the scope to all energy-related products; and the 2017 Regulation digitized the system and added QR codes [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3]. ## Legal and enforcement context

The legal basis for energy efficiency information requirements is rooted in the **Energy Labelling Framework**, which was established by **Directive 2010/30/EU** and later replaced by **Regulation (EU) 2017/1369** [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The current framework is described as setting out a **framework for energy-related products placed on the market or put into service** and providing for the **indication by labeling** and **standard product information** [N6-R4]. The 2010/30/EU Directive was itself a **harmonisation of national measures on end-user information**, particularly through labeling [N6-R1]. The framework therefore provides the **legal basis** for requiring suppliers and dealers to supply and display labels, and it is the main rule governing energy efficiency information across the EU [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Under the framework, the European Commission has a central role. It is empowered to adopt **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. The 2017 Regulation also requires the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database** and to register each product model in that database [N6-R2]. Suppliers are obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. This shows that the Commission’s role is not merely advisory: it is responsible for **setting rules, maintaining a product database, and ensuring that product information is available for verification** [N6-R2].

Member States have **supervision and enforcement mechanisms** under the framework. The 1992 Directive required Member States to implement energy labeling measures for the listed household appliances, and the 2017 Regulation continues this obligation through the registration and verification system [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the Commission has organized **Implementation Dialogues** and **Reality Checks** to assess the current framework and prepare simplification proposals [N5-F4]. This suggests that enforcement and compliance are monitored through both national implementation and Commission-led review processes.

The European Commission and EU institutions interact through the **framework and delegated regulation mechanism**. The Commission adopts the **main framework regulation** and **secondary delegated regulations** that apply directly in Member States [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The Commission also interacts with market surveillance authorities, as suppliers must make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. ## 1) Chronology and major directive milestones

The earliest stage in the EU’s energy-efficiency labeling history was a **1976 Council recommendation** on the rational use of energy for electrical household appliances. This recommendation was the first EU-level measure to address public information on appliance energy use and recommended standardized labels for selected household appliances such as water heaters, cookers, refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, ovens, and lighting sources [N1-F1]. It laid the conceptual foundation for later directives.

A major milestone was the **1979 Framework Energy Labelling Directive**, which established the general rules of the energy labeling framework but was **not mandatory/EU-wide**; Member States could choose whether to implement it [N1-F1]. The directive covered selected household appliances and introduced a general label template, while specific implementation rules were left to later directives [N1-F1]. This marked the first formal EU-wide energy labeling framework.

The next key expansion came in **1992 with Directive 92/75/EEC**, which made the framework **mandatory for selected household appliances** and required suppliers to provide a product fiche [N1-F1]. This directive laid the foundation for the modern label and product information system [N1-F1]. In **1994**, the framework was extended to refrigerators, freezers, and their combinations with a new label design that introduced the **energy efficiency scale** using letters A to G and a colour code [N1-F1]. This became the recognizable design still used today [N1-F1].

The next major milestone was the **2010/30/EU Energy Labelling Framework**, which extended the scope from household appliances to **all energy-related products**, defined as goods that have an impact on energy consumption during use [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The directive empowered the Commission to adopt secondary legislation through **delegated regulations** directly applicable in Member States under certain conditions [N1-F1]. It also established a harmonised system for end-user information, particularly by means of labeling [N6-R1]. This was a major expansion because it moved the regime from a limited household-appliance set to a much broader product universe.

The current regime became a **Regulation** in **2017 with Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, which replaced the 2010/30/EU Directive and introduced a digital framework [N6-R2]. The Regulation required the Commission to establish and maintain a **product database**, and suppliers were obliged to register each product model in the database and make technical documentation available for national authorities verifying compliance [N6-R2]. The 2017 Regulation also introduced **QR codes** on labels, making the label more digitally visible [N3-F3].

Since then, the framework has continued to evolve. In **2021**, the label underwent a major rescaling, reintroducing a simpler classification using only letters A to G and changing how products were classified [N3-F3]. The Commission is also currently examining ways to simplify legislation on energy-efficient products, with a call for evidence on the Energy Labelling Framework Regulation and related rules [N5-F4]. This shows that the framework remains under active review, even as the 2017 Regulation has already become the current governing rule [N6-R2].
